Since adjacent effective edge normals are linearly independent at a genuine corner, stationarity forces both coefficients of these two affine test functions to vanish. Rescaling \(s/\ell_E\) gives the displayed moments.

The domain-independent Dirichlet heat-kernel estimate gives \(\|u\|_\infty^2\le e^2\lambda/(8\pi)\) for the normalized first eigenfunction. Under the edge-moment hypotheses, @lem-airy-identity applies, and \(\int_Pu^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\int_Pu^2=\|u\|_\infty^2\); combining these facts yields \[ \int_P|\nabla u|^4\le \frac{e^2\lambda^3}{8\pi}. \] The same \(L^\infty\) bound gives \(\int_P|u|^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\), so the \(W^{1,4}(P)\) norm is bounded by a constant depending only on \(A_0\) and \(\Lambda\). Since \(u\in H^1_0(P)\), its zero extension has no boundary distribution term in its weak gradient; the extension therefore lies in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) with the same gradient bound. Morrey’s inequality in dimension two then gives a \(C^{0,1/2}\) representative with the same parameter dependence.

For the quantitative rate, write the pulled-back eigenproblem as \[ -\Delta v=\lambda|1+g|^2v,\qquad v|_{\partial\mathbb D}=0, \] with the weighted \(L^2\) normalization. Put \(d(z)=1-|z|\). For \(g\in A^2\) with no constant or linear term, the Bergman pointwise estimate gives \(|g(z)|\le C\|g\|_{A^2}/d(z)\). Consequently, Hardy’s inequality gives, for all \(\varphi,\psi\in H^1_0(\mathbb D)\), \[ \left|\int_{\mathbb D}2\operatorname{Re}(g)\varphi\psiight|\le C\sqrt S\,\|\varphi\|_{H^1_0}\|\psi\|_{H^1_0},\qquad \left|\int_{\mathbb D}|g|^2\varphi\psiight|\le CS\,\|\varphi\|_{H^1_0}\|\psi\|_{H^1_0}. \] Indeed \(|g|^2\le CS/d^2\), \(\int|\varphi|^2/d^2\le4\int|

The simple disk eigenvalue is isolated by a fixed spectral gap, so the real-analytic form perturbation theorem applies uniformly to this family.Write \(g=t h\) with \(t=\sqrt S\) and \(\|h\|_{A^2}=1\). The simple disk eigenvalue is isolated by a fixed spectral gap. The form version of analytic simple-eigenvalue perturbation therefore gives, uniformly in such \(h\), \[ v=v_0+t v_1+t^2v_2+O_{H^1_0}(t^3), \qquad \lambda= j^2+t\lambda_1+t^2\lambda_2+O(t^3). \] The first variation is \(\lambda_1=-j^2\int_{\mathbb D}(h+ ar h)v_0^2=0\) because \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient. Write \(v_0(r)=J_0(jr)/(\sqrt\pi J_1(j))\) and \(p_D=j/\sqrt\pi\). For the real mode \(h=a z^n\), the first-order equation in the \(n\)th angular sector has the explicit solution \[ v_1(r,	heta)=a w_n(r)\cos(n	heta),\qquad w_n(r)= rac{r^{n+1}v_0'(r)+p_DJ_n(jr)/J_n(j)}{n+1}. \] The Bessel equation verifies the radial equation and \(w_n(1)=0\). Orthogonality of distinct angular modes and density of analytic polynomials extend the formula to every \(h\in A^2\). Since \(A(P)=\pi(1+S)\) in @def-conformal-data, this yields the uniform expansion \[  rac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}). \] The perturbed branch remains the first eigenvalue because its eigenfunction is the positive continuation of the disk ground state and the form perturbation is smaller than the fixed spectral gap. The first-order equation and the uniform form estimates also give \(

Thus the displayed gradient expansion in the statement holds. Since \(0<ho_n<2\), the quadratic term is at least \(S/3\); after shrinking the universal small neighborhood, \(J(P)/(\pi j^2)-1\ge S/6\). This proves the uniform perturbation expansion and coercivity.

Use the similarity invariance in @def-j-functional to normalize \(A(P)=\pi\) and translate so that the Fraenkel-optimal comparison disk is \(D=B_1(0)\). The regular-polygon asymptotic is \[ \frac{J(R_M)}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{M^3}+O(M^{-5}). \] The upper bound and the displayed asymptotic give \(\lambda_1(P)\le j^2(1+CN^{-3})\), while Faber–Krahn gives \(\lambda_1(P)\ge j^2\). Quantitative Faber–Krahn therefore gives \(|P\triangle D|\to0\). Let \(u_N\) be the normalized positive eigenfunction and extend it by zero. By @lem-uniform-w14, the extensions are uniformly bounded in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) and hence equicontinuous and uniformly bounded. Arzelà–Ascoli gives a locally uniform limit along a subsequence. On every compact set outside \(\overline D\), the limit must vanish: otherwise the uniform Hölder bound would force a fixed positive amount of area in \(P_N\setminus D\), contradicting \(|P_N\triangle D|\to0\). The same argument gives zero trace on \(\partial D\). Since \(\|u_N\|_\infty\) is uniformly bounded, the mass outside \(D\) tends to zero; hence the limit has \(L^2(D)\) norm one. Weak lower semicontinuity gives \(\int_D|\nabla u|^2\le\liminf\lambda_1(P_N)=j^2\), while the disk Rayleigh inequality gives the reverse inequality. Thus the limit is the normalized positive disk eigenfunction \(u_0\). Uniqueness of the limit upgrades the whole sequence to local uniform convergence, and the boundary Hölder bound upgrades it to uniform convergence on \(\overline D\). Since \(u_0>0\) on \(B_{1-\eta}\), eventually \(u_N>0\) there; because the zero extension vanishes off \(P_N\), \(B_{1-\eta}\subset P_N\).The maximal conformal radius is at least \(1-\eta\) by monotonicity under inclusion and at most \(1\) by the conformal area inequality \(A(P)\ge\pi r_P^2\). In the normalization of @def-conformal-data, \(1+S=r_P^{-2}\to1\).By @lem-disk-perturbation, once \(N\) is large enough that \(S\le S_0\), the uniform expansion and coercivity give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}-1\ge S/6. \] The regular-polygon upper bound is \(O(N^{-3})\), hence \(S\le CN^{-3}\) with a universal constant.

Under the edge-moment hypotheses @lem-edge-moments, pull @lem-airy-identity back by \(F\) and use \(F'^{-1}=1+k\) to obtain \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v|^4|1+k|^2 =\lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2- rac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)}. \] The normalization in @def-conformal-data gives \(k(0)=0\), hence the constant Fourier coefficient of \(k\) is zero, and \(k=-g/(1+g)\). On every fixed disk \(|z|\le r_0<1\), the Bergman pointwise estimate gives \(|g|\le C\sqrt S\) and hence \(|k|\le C\sqrt S\) when \(S\) is small. The expansion supplied by @lem-disk-perturbation and the form perturbation argument in its proof give, in the weighted integrals below, \[ |
abla v|^4=a+b_1+R_1, \qquad a=|
abla v_0|^4, \qquad \int_0^{2\pi}b_1(r,	heta)\,d	heta=0, \qquad \|R_1\|_{L^1(\mathbb D)}\le CS. \] The function \(a\) is radial and satisfies \(a\ge c_0>0\) on a fixed annulus \(A_0\subset\mathbb D\). Expanding the left side and using the zero circular mean of \(b_1\) gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v|^4|1+k|^2 \ge \int_{\mathbb D}a+c_0T-C\{S+\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+ST\}. \] Here the \(\sqrt S\sqrt T\) term is the \(b_1\operatorname{Re}k\) pairing, the \(\sqrt S T\) term is the \(b_1|k|^2\) pairing, and the remaining terms use \(\|R_1\|_{L^1}\le CS\) and \(|k|\le C\sqrt S\) on \(|z|\le r_0\). The same form expansion for \(v^4|1+g|^2\) and \(\lambda\) gives \[ \lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2- rac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)} \le \int_{\mathbb D}a+C\{S+\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+ST\}. \] Subtracting these two estimates in the pulled-back identity yields \[ T\le C\{S+\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+ST\}. \] Young’s inequality absorbs the mixed term and, for sufficiently small \(S\), the last two terms, proving \(T\le CS\).

The first-order perturbation and the second-order disk calculation from @lem-disk-perturbation give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\rho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}), \] with \(\beta_n=n+1-\rho_n\). By @lem-inverse-energy, \(T\le CS\). The identity \(g+k=-gk\) gives weighted coefficient bounds; splitting at \(K=S^{-1/2}\) yields, for every multiplier \(O((n+1)^{-2})\), \[ \left|\sum b_n(|k_n|^2-|g_n|^2)\right|\le CS^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] The same bound replaces \(g\) by \(L=\log F'\) in all such quadratic forms, while the leading \(T-S\) term is retained.To compute that leading term, introduce the Airy potential from @lem-airy-identity and the two-variable analytic functional obtained by treating \(g\) and \(k\) independently. Its quadratic part is computed on a polynomial direction \(F'(z)=1+ta z^n\). The first-order boundary flux is \[ \delta(q-c)=-\frac{2p_D^2\beta_n}{n+1}\operatorname{Re}(ae^{in\theta}), \qquad p_D=j/\sqrt\pi. \] The induced first-order Airy gradient has frequencies \(n+1\) and \(1-n\); its signed area is \(-\pi d_n^2/[8(n^2-1)]\). Since the Airy identity equals minus four times this area, the quadratic contribution is \[ 2\pi p_D^4\frac{\beta_n^2}{(n+1)^2(n^2-1)}|a|^2. \] Rotational orthogonality removes cross terms, and density of analytic polynomials extends the calculation to \(A^2\). The actual relation \(g+k=-gk\) then gives \[ S-T=2\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n^2}{(n+1)^2(n^2-1)}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}). \] The logarithmic inequality \[ \|L\|_{A^2}^2\le (S+T)/2 \] comes from \(|f|^2+|f|^{-2}-2\ge4(\operatorname{Re}L)^2\) and equality of real and imaginary Bergman energies. Combining these formulas gives \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n}{(n+1)^2}\left(1+\frac{\beta_n}{n^2-1}\right)|L_n|^2-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] Finally @def-turn-measure gives \(L_n=2\widehat\mu(n)/n\), which is the claimed inequality.

Define on \(\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)\) the self-adjoint matrix \[ A_{rs}=\tau^{(r+s)/2}\widehat\mu(r-s)=\sum_iw_i(v_i)_r\overline{(v_i)_s}, \qquad (v_i)_r=\tau^{r/2}e^{-ir\theta_i}. \] The Vandermonde vectors at distinct nodes are linearly independent, so \(A\) has exactly \(p\) positive eigenvalues \(\alpha_1\ge\cdots\ge\alpha_p>0\). The trace is \((1-\tau)^{-1}\), and the negative eigenvalues can only decrease the trace, hence \(Q:=\sum_i\alpha_i\ge(1-\tau)^{-1}\). The shift compression and the min–max principle give \(\alpha_{i+1}\le\tau\alpha_i\). For fixed \(Q\) and these ratio constraints, a finite exchange argument (move mass from an earlier coordinate to the latest coordinate until the active constraint is met) shows that the minimum of the strictly convex function \(\sum_i\alpha_i^2\) is attained at \[ \alpha_i=Q\frac{(1-\tau)\tau^{i-1}}{1-\tau^p},\qquad 1\le i\le p. \] Consequently \[ \sum_i\alpha_i^2\ge Q^2\frac{1-\tau}{1+\tau}\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p} \ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{(1-\tau^2)(1-\tau^p)}. \] On the other hand, \[ \|A\|_{HS}^2=\frac{1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2}{1-\tau^2} \] and the Hilbert–Schmidt norm dominates the squared positive eigenvalues. Rearranging gives \[ 1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2\ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p}, \] which is exactly the claimed bound.

The Bessel bounds \(5.78<j^2<5.8\) give \(1.89<\kappa<1.9\). The recurrence for \(J_n\) implies \(0<\rho_n<2\) and, for \(n\ge3\), \(\rho_n<n\alpha/(n^2+\kappa)\) with \(\alpha=\kappa+1\). Substitution into \[ a_n=\frac{n-\rho_n+\rho_n^2/(n+1)^2}{n^2(n^2-1)} \] proves \(a_n\ge b_n\); for \(n=2\), the identity \(J_0(j)=0\) reduces the inequality to \(\kappa^3+7\kappa^2+12\kappa-54\ge0\), which holds for \(\kappa\ge1.89\).The Laplace representation follows from \[ \int_0^\infty e^{-nt}(1-\cos(\sqrt\kappa t))\,dt=\frac{\kappa}{n(n^2+\kappa)}. \] Apply @lem-toeplitz-positive-atoms with \(\tau=e^{-t}\) and integrate against the nonnegative weight \((1-\cos(\sqrt\kappa t))/\kappa\). Tonelli’s theorem gives \(E_b(\mu)\ge B_p\).

By @lem-spectral-core and @lem-kernel-comparison, \(a_n\ge b_n\) for \(n\ge2\). The missing \(n=1\) term is harmless because @def-turn-measure gives \(\widehat\mu(1)=0\). Hence \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge 1+4E_b(\mu)-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] The lower bound \(E_b(\mu)\ge B_p\) is exactly @lem-kernel-comparison.

If there are at least two reflex corners, the number \(p\) of convex corners is at most \(N-2\). By @lem-near-circle-conformal, \(S\le CN^{-3}\), and @lem-signed-turn-lower-bound gives \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+4B_{N-2}-o(N^{-4}). \] The estimate \(B_p\ge\zeta(3)p^{-3}-\kappa\zeta(5)p^{-5}\) and the regular-polygon asymptotic in @lem-near-circle-conformal imply \[ 4B_{N-2}-\frac{4\zeta(3)}{(N-1)^3}=12\zeta(3)N^{-4}+O(N^{-5})>0 \] for large \(N\), so the assumed upper bound is impossible.

The boundary identity in @def-conformal-data gives a homogeneous \(H^{1/2}\) seminorm of \(F-F(0)-z\) equal to \(S\); restricting it to a straight prevertex arc of length \(\varepsilon\) gives a lower bound \(c\varepsilon^4\), hence every prevertex gap is at most \(CS^{1/4}\). The boundary derivative estimate accompanying @lem-disk-perturbation gives for the disk boundary derivative \(p=-\partial_rv\) on every such arc \[ \operatorname{osc}_I p\le C\{\sqrt S\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(e/\varepsilon)}+S\}\le CS^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \]Place the unique negative turn at angle \(0\). The cotangent formula for \(\ell=\log|F'|\) shows that, on one of the adjacent edges selected according to the sign of the constant term, \(|F'|\) is monotone and the logarithmic drop across a central subarc is at least \(c(a+v)\), where \(-v\) is the reflex weight and \(a\) is the selected adjacent positive weight. For the decreasing function \(h=|F'|\), define \[ \mathsf A=\int_{s<t}h(s)/h(t)\,dsdt,\qquad \mathsf B=\int_{s<t}h(t)/h(s)\,dsdt. \] A four-rectangle comparison gives \[ \frac{\mathsf A-\mathsf B}{\mathsf A+\mathsf B}\ge c(a+v). \] Put \(k_0=h^{-2}\) and normalize the selected edge to \(x\in[0,1]\). The identity equating \(D\) with a first moment of \(k_0\) is not valid for a general monotone \(h\); the needed valid substitute is the following elementary one-dimensional estimate: \[ D=\frac{\int_{s<t}(h(s)/h(t)-h(t)/h(s))\,dsdt}{\int_{s<t}(h(s)/h(t)+h(t)/h(s))\,dsdt},\quad \int_0^1(x-1/2)p(x)^2k_0(x)\,dx=0 \Longrightarrow D\le C\frac{\max_Ip-\min_Ip}{\min_Ip}. \] To verify it, write the numerator and denominator with \(k_0=h^{-2}\), split the square into the four rectangles determined by \(x=1/2\), and use monotonicity of \(k_0\); the centered-moment equation replaces every occurrence of \(\int(x-1/2)k_0\) by \(-\int(x-1/2)(p^2-p_*^2)k_0\), while the denominator is bounded below by the same positive rectangle integrals. Since \(p\ge p_D/2\) uniformly, this gives \(D\le C\operatorname{osc}_I p\). The lower bound \(D\ge c(a+v)\) and the last inequality imply \(a+v\le C S^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). Combining this with \(S\le CN^{-3}\) proves the stated bound.

Let \(\delta=E_b(\mu)-B_{N-1}\ge0\). By @lem-signed-turn-lower-bound, the assumed upper bound and the regular-polygon asymptotic imply \[ \delta\le CN^{-9/2}\sqrt{\log N}. \] For \(U_b(\theta)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_n\operatorname{Re}(\widehat\mu(n)e^{in\theta})\), the Laplace representation in @def-positive-kernel and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[ \|U_b\|_\infty\le C\sqrt\delta+CN^{-5/2}. \] The exact expansion is \[ E_b(\widetilde\mu)-E_b(\mu)= \frac{2a(E_b(\mu)-U_b(\theta_*))+a^2(K_b(0)-E_b(\mu))}{(1-a)^2}, \] where \(K_b(0)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_n\). Since @lem-single-reflex-small-atom gives \(a=O(N^{-9/4}\sqrt{\log N})\) and \(E_b(\mu)=O(N^{-3})\), the right side is \(O(N^{-9/2}\log N)=o(N^{-4})\).

Assume the conclusion fails. If there are at least two reflex corners, @lem-two-reflex-exclusion gives a contradiction. Thus there is exactly one reflex corner. Apply @lem-single-reflex-small-atom and @lem-atom-deletion. The deleted measure has \(N-2\) positive atoms, and @lem-kernel-comparison yields \(E_b(\widetilde\mu)\ge B_{N-2}\). By the proof of @lem-signed-turn-lower-bound (equivalently, by @lem-spectral-core together with @lem-kernel-comparison), \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+4E_b(\mu)-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] Using @lem-atom-deletion and \(S\le CN^{-3}\) from @lem-near-circle-conformal gives \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+4B_{N-2}-o(N^{-4}). \] The regular-polygon asymptotic gives \[ \frac{J(R_{N-1})}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{(N-1)^3}+O(N^{-5}), \] while \(B_{N-2}=\zeta(3)(N-2)^{-3}+O(N^{-5})\). Their difference is \(12\zeta(3)N^{-4}+O(N^{-5})\), contradicting \(J(P)\le J(R_{N-1})\) for large \(N\).

report.summary: The construction is meaningful and defines the stated objects. Finite cyclic deletion terminates, preserves the boundary, and yields a unique maximal straight-segment decomposition; the area is well-defined.

results.statement_text: An admissible polygon is a bounded simple planar polygonal domain whose boundary is a simple cyclic union of finitely many nonzero straight segments, with no self-contact. A genuine corner is a boundary vertex at which the two incident directed segments are not collinear; its interior angle is required to lie strictly between \(0\) and \(2\pi\). Starting from any polygonal presentation, delete adjacent collinear redundant vertices cyclically until no such vertex remains; the resulting effective-edge count is the invariant number \(N\), and \(A(P)\) is the Euclidean area. The cyclic deletion is independent of deletion order because it removes exactly the vertices at which the incoming and outgoing segment directions agree.
results.title: Admissible simple polygon

gaps: The existence and interior attainment of a maximal conformal radius, together with the corresponding centered Riemann map, are asserted without identifying the standard theorem that the conformal-radius function is continuous and tends to zero at the boundary of a bounded polygonal domain.

The A^2 claims rely tersely on standard conformal change-of-variables/Parseval facts for F' and on Schwarz–Christoffel boundary asymptotics at all boundary points; the argument only sketches the prevertex estimate and does not explicitly account for regular edge points.
nonblocking_comments: The first-order condition F''(0)=0, the normalization giving \widetilde F'(0)=1, the coefficient formula for S, the area identity, and g+k=-gk are correct.
Similarity normalization preserves J and effective-edge count under the stated definitions.

report.summary: The construction is mathematically coherent: the normalization, Taylor expansion, area identity, algebraic relation, and inverse-derivative integrability claim are valid for an admissible polygon. A few standard existence and boundary-regularity facts are used without explicit justification.

results.statement_text: For a polygon \(P\) in @def-admissible-polygon, let \(r_P\) be its maximal conformal radius and choose a Riemann map \(F:\mathbb D\to P\) centered at a maximizing point, with \(F'(0)=r_P>0\) and \(F''(0)=0\). The equality \(F''(0)=0\) is the first-order condition for the maximum of \((1-|a|^2)|F'(a)|\). Replace \(P\) by the similarity-normalized polygon \(\widetilde P=r_P^{-1}(P-F(0))\) and write \(\widetilde F=r_P^{-1}(F-F(0))\); by the similarity invariance of \(J\) in @def-j-functional, this leaves \(J\) and the effective-edge count unchanged and gives \(\widetilde F'(0)=1\). In the normalized notation, \[ \widetilde F'(z)=1+g(z),\qquad g(z)=\sum_{n\ge2}g_nz^n. \] Set \[ S=\|g\|_{A^2}^2=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|g_n|^2}{n+1},\qquad T=\|(\widetilde F')^{-1}-1\|_{A^2}^2,\qquad \|h\|_{A^2}^2=\pi^{-1}\int_{\mathbb D}|h|^2dA. \] The area identity is \(A(\widetilde P)=\pi(1+S)\); all later uses of \(P,F,A,\lambda_1\) are understood in this similarity-normalized representative. Write \(k=(\widetilde F')^{-1}-1\), so \(T=\|k\|_{A^2}^2\) and \(g+k=-gk\). The inverse derivative is in \(A^2\): at a prevertex with interior angle \(\omega\in(0,2\pi)\), the Schwarz–Christoffel exponent is \(\alpha=\omega/\pi-1<1\), so \(|(\widetilde F')^{-1}|^2=O(r^{-2\alpha})\) and its area integral is bounded by \(C\int_0^\varepsilon r^{1-2\alpha}\,dr<\infty\).

Uniqueness of the limit upgrades the whole sequence to local uniform convergence, and the boundary Hölder bound upgrades it to uniform convergence on \(\overline D\). Since \(u_0>0\) on \(B_{1-\eta}\), eventually \(u_N>0\) there; because the zero extension vanishes off \(P_N\), \(B_{1-\eta}\subset P_N\).The maximal conformal radius is at least \(1-\eta\) by monotonicity under inclusion and at most \(1\) by the conformal area inequality \(A(P)\ge\pi r_P^2\). In the normalization of @def-conformal-data, \(1+S=r_P^{-2}\to1\).By @lem-disk-perturbation, once \(N\) is large enough that \(S\le S_0\), the uniform expansion and coercivity give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}-1\ge S/6. \] The regular-polygon upper bound is \(O(N^{-3})\), hence \(S\le CN^{-3}\) with a universal constant.

results.proof_text: The boundary identity in @def-conformal-data gives a homogeneous \(H^{1/2}\) seminorm of \(F-F(0)-z\) equal to \(S\); restricting it to a straight prevertex arc of length \(\varepsilon\) gives a lower bound \(c\varepsilon^4\), hence every prevertex gap is at most \(CS^{1/4}\). The boundary derivative estimate accompanying @lem-disk-perturbation gives for the disk boundary derivative \(p=-\partial_rv\) on every such arc \[ \operatorname{osc}_I p\le C\{\sqrt S\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(e/\varepsilon)}+S\}\le CS^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \]Place the unique negative turn at angle \(0\). The cotangent formula for \(\ell=\log|F'|\) shows that, on one of the adjacent edges selected according to the sign of the constant term, \(|F'|\) is monotone and the logarithmic drop across a central subarc is at least \(c(a+v)\), where \(-v\) is the reflex weight and \(a\) is the selected adjacent positive weight. For the decreasing function \(h=|F'|\), define \[ \mathsf A=\int_{s<t}h(s)/h(t)\,dsdt,\qquad \mathsf B=\int_{s<t}h(t)/h(s)\,dsdt. \] A four-rectangle comparison gives \[ \frac{\mathsf A-\mathsf B}{\mathsf A+\mathsf B}\ge c(a+v). \] Put \(k_0=h^{-2}\) and normalize the selected edge to \(x\in[0,1]\). The identity equating \(D\) with a first moment of \(k_0\) is not valid for a general monotone \(h\); the needed valid substitute is the following elementary one-dimensional estimate: \[ D=\frac{\int_{s<t}(h(s)/h(t)-h(t)/h(s))\,dsdt}{\int_{s<t}(h(s)/h(t)+h(t)/h(s))\,dsdt},\quad \int_0^1(x-1/2)p(x)^2k_0(x)\,dx=0 \Longrightarrow D\le C\frac{\max_Ip-\min_Ip}{\min_Ip}. \] To verify it, write the numerator and denominator with \(k_0=h^{-2}\), split the square into the four rectangles determined by \(x=1/2\), and use monotonicity of \(k_0\); the centered-moment equation replaces every occurrence of \(\int(x-1/2)k_0\) by \(-\int(x-1/2)(p^2-p_*^2)k_0\), while the denominator is bounded below by the same positive rectangle integrals. Since \(p\ge p_D/2\) uniformly, this gives \(D\le C\operatorname{osc}_I p\). The lower bound \(D\ge c(a+v)\) and the last inequality imply \(a+v\le C S^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). Combining this with \(S\le CN^{-3}\) proves the stated bound.

results.proof_text: The first-order perturbation and the second-order disk calculation from @lem-disk-perturbation give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\rho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}), \] with \(\beta_n=n+1-\rho_n\). By @lem-inverse-energy, \(T\le CS\). The identity \(g+k=-gk\) gives weighted coefficient bounds; splitting at \(K=S^{-1/2}\) yields, for every multiplier \(O((n+1)^{-2})\), \[ \left|\sum b_n(|k_n|^2-|g_n|^2)\right|\le CS^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] The same bound replaces \(g\) by \(L=\log F'\) in all such quadratic forms, while the leading \(T-S\) term is retained.To compute that leading term, introduce the Airy potential from @lem-airy-identity and the two-variable analytic functional obtained by treating \(g\) and \(k\) independently. Its quadratic part is computed on a polynomial direction \(F'(z)=1+ta z^n\). The first-order boundary flux is \[ \delta(q-c)=-\frac{2p_D^2\beta_n}{n+1}\operatorname{Re}(ae^{in\theta}), \qquad p_D=j/\sqrt\pi. \] The induced first-order Airy gradient has frequencies \(n+1\) and \(1-n\); its signed area is \(-\pi d_n^2/[8(n^2-1)]\). Since the Airy identity equals minus four times this area, the quadratic contribution is \[ 2\pi p_D^4\frac{\beta_n^2}{(n+1)^2(n^2-1)}|a|^2. \] Rotational orthogonality removes cross terms, and density of analytic polynomials extends the calculation to \(A^2\). The actual relation \(g+k=-gk\) then gives \[ S-T=2\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n^2}{(n+1)^2(n^2-1)}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}). \] The logarithmic inequality \[ \|L\|_{A^2}^2\le (S+T)/2 \] comes from \(|f|^2+|f|^{-2}-2\ge4(\operatorname{Re}L)^2\) and equality of real and imaginary Bergman energies. Combining these formulas gives \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n}{(n+1)^2}\left(1+\frac{\beta_n}{n^2-1}\right)|L_n|^2-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] Finally @def-turn-measure gives \(L_n=2\widehat\mu(n)/n\), which is the claimed inequality.

results.proof_text: Define on \(\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)\) the self-adjoint matrix \[ A_{rs}=\tau^{(r+s)/2}\widehat\mu(r-s)=\sum_iw_i(v_i)_r\overline{(v_i)_s}, \qquad (v_i)_r=\tau^{r/2}e^{-ir\theta_i}. \] The Vandermonde vectors at distinct nodes are linearly independent, so \(A\) has exactly \(p\) positive eigenvalues \(\alpha_1\ge\cdots\ge\alpha_p>0\). The trace is \((1-\tau)^{-1}\), and the negative eigenvalues can only decrease the trace, hence \(Q:=\sum_i\alpha_i\ge(1-\tau)^{-1}\). The shift compression and the min–max principle give \(\alpha_{i+1}\le\tau\alpha_i\). For fixed \(Q\) and these ratio constraints, a finite exchange argument (move mass from an earlier coordinate to the latest coordinate until the active constraint is met) shows that the minimum of the strictly convex function \(\sum_i\alpha_i^2\) is attained at \[ \alpha_i=Q\frac{(1-\tau)\tau^{i-1}}{1-\tau^p},\qquad 1\le i\le p. \] Consequently \[ \sum_i\alpha_i^2\ge Q^2\frac{1-\tau}{1+\tau}\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p} \ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{(1-\tau^2)(1-\tau^p)}. \] On the other hand, \[ \|A\|_{HS}^2=\frac{1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2}{1-\tau^2} \] and the Hilbert–Schmidt norm dominates the squared positive eigenvalues. Rearranging gives \[ 1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2\ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p}, \] which is exactly the claimed bound.
results.statement_text: Let \(\mu\) be a finite real atomic measure of total mass \(1\) with exactly \(p\) positive atoms, allowing arbitrary negative atoms. For \(0<\tau<1\), \[ \sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2\ge\frac{\tau^p}{1-\tau^p}. \]

results.proof_text: The domain-independent Dirichlet heat-kernel estimate gives \(\|u\|_\infty^2\le e^2\lambda/(8\pi)\) for the normalized first eigenfunction. Under the edge-moment hypotheses, @lem-airy-identity applies, and \(\int_Pu^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\int_Pu^2=\|u\|_\infty^2\); combining these facts yields \[ \int_P|\nabla u|^4\le \frac{e^2\lambda^3}{8\pi}. \] The same \(L^\infty\) bound gives \(\int_P|u|^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\), so the \(W^{1,4}(P)\) norm is bounded by a constant depending only on \(A_0\) and \(\Lambda\). Since \(u\in H^1_0(P)\), its zero extension has no boundary distribution term in its weak gradient; the extension therefore lies in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) with the same gradient bound. Morrey’s inequality in dimension two then gives a \(C^{0,1/2}\) representative with the same parameter dependence.
